claims.proposition_evaluated: Among replacement dwelling units on Edmonton lots where one dwelling was demolished under a 2016-2025 residential demolition permit, more than 50 percent had a higher constant-dollar assessed value on the first full roll after completion than the demolished dwelling's total assessed value on the roll in force in the year before demolition. I applied the brief's own-total-value rule to separately titled dwellings and its building-total-divided-by-dwelling-count rule to units in single-title buildings.
claims.interpretation_notes: The circulating $350,000-to-$1,000,000 example is not testable without an address or source and was not treated as a threshold. Aggregate title and lot values do not test the proposition. The closest published Edmonton analysis uses lot totals and a different cohort, and its result cannot be converted into the required unit-level share.

supporting_evidence.finding: A non-government analysis matched Edmonton permits to assessments and found a median gross lot-level assessed-value uplift of $1.7 million across 67 completed, 2024-permitted mature-area lots containing five or more replacement units. It found $1.1 million for 27 five-to-six-unit lots and $1.9 million for 40 lots with seven or more units.
supporting_evidence.establishes: Selected aggregate lot assessments often rose after redevelopment. It does not establish the required replacement-dwelling-unit share because it uses lot totals, a 2024 RS-zone cohort, a mature-area geography, and different matching and inclusion rules.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City estimates each property's open-market value annually as of July 1 of the preceding year and records physical condition as of December 31.
supporting_evidence.establishes: The City's assessments are market-value estimates and support the brief's July valuation-date convention. They do not identify which roll was the first full roll for each replacement.

challenging_evidence.finding: The 2024 City infill report says 286 new single-detached houses were built while 387 were demolished in the redeveloping area, a net loss of 101, and concludes that other built forms were replacing demolished detached houses.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Multi-unit replacement is material, so an increase in a whole lot's value cannot be assumed to mean that each replacement unit exceeds the demolished dwelling's value. The report contains no matched price comparison.

challenging_evidence.finding: The General Building Permits dataset lacks a parcel identifier and publishes residential occupancy dates only for permits finalized from 2022 onward. The historical assessment dataset reports total assessed value but not title structure or dwelling count within a title.
challenging_evidence.source_title: General Building Permits and Historical Property Assessment Data
challenging_evidence.establishes: The public permit data alone cannot reliably identify the first full post-completion roll for much of the cohort or calculate building-average value per dwelling without another source.

challenging_evidence.finding: The historical assessment dataset covers 2012-2025 and includes account number, assessment year, address, legal description, coordinates, year built, lot size and total assessed value. It does not publish land and improvement components, self-contained dwelling counts, or an explicit separately-titled versus single-title classification.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Several fields required to construct the verdict measure are absent from the public assessment table.

limitations: No source reports the required city-wide unit-level numerator, denominator, bounds, median ratio, quartiles or range.
No source reports the same result for the frozen 2023-12-31 Mature Neighbourhood Overlay boundary or the City Plan redeveloping-area sensitivity.
Completion dates before 2022 are generally absent from the public permit dataset, preventing consistent identification of the first full assessment roll.
Legal descriptions, addresses, assessment accounts and title boundaries can change when lots are split or consolidated. The public data do not provide a verified historical parcel crosswalk.
The closest published Edmonton analysis uses lot totals and divides old baselines among split child lots. Both choices differ from the frozen proposition.

No complete reporting was found for fire-order and safety-order demolitions, multiple-dwelling demolitions, tenure changes, prior rents, displacement, sale-to-sale sensitivity or missing-data attrition.
The required CPI and New Housing Price Index series exist, but no property-level series was available to adjust.
unknowns: How many 2016-2025 residential demolition permits involved exactly one existing dwelling.
How many permits can be matched reliably to completed replacement housing and the correct pre-demolition assessment.
The number of self-contained replacement dwellings on each title.
Whether more than half of all eligible replacement units exceed the full demolished-dwelling value after inflation adjustment.
Whether the result differs city-wide, inside the historical Mature Neighbourhood Overlay, or under the five-year cohort.
How unmatched and unclassified cases affect the lower and upper bounds.

missing_evidence.description: A verified crosswalk linking every eligible demolition to replacement parcels, titles and assessment accounts through address changes, subdivisions and consolidations.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Development Services and Assessment and Taxation, supplemented by Alberta Land Titles or AltaLIS

missing_evidence.description: Completion and occupancy dates before 2022 sufficient to identify each replacement's first full assessment roll.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton permit and inspection systems

missing_evidence.description: Verified self-contained dwelling count and title structure for every replacement, including secondary suites.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton permit records, Alberta Land Titles and property owners

missing_evidence.description: Fire-order and safety-order status, prior tenure, prior rent and recorded tenant displacement.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: City of Edmonton Fire Rescue Services, Development Services, property owners and tenants

calculations_needed: Build the 2016-2025 residential demolition frame and report attrition at every matching step.
Exclude lots with more than one demolished dwelling from the verdict denominator while reporting them separately.
Identify each replacement title and dwelling count, then calculate own total value or building-average value per dwelling as prescribed.
Adjust both assessment dates to July 2025 dollars with Edmonton monthly all-items CPI and repeat with annual CPI and Edmonton New Housing Price Index.
Calculate the unit-level share and bounds, ratio distribution, every-replacement lot share and at-least-one-replacement lot share.
Repeat for the historical Mature Neighbourhood Overlay, City Plan redeveloping area, five-year cohort and fire-order-excluded sensitivity.
what_would_change_my_verdict: A reproducible complete-frame analysis showing that the lower bound exceeds 50 percent would change the verdict to Supported.
A reproducible analysis showing that the upper bound is 50 percent or less would change the verdict to Contradicted.
Publication of the missing parcel crosswalk, completion dates and dwelling-per-title counts could make either threshold calculation possible.
claims.suggested_one_line: Public Edmonton data make a partial reconstruction possible, but they do not establish whether more than half of replacement dwelling units exceed the demolished dwelling's inflation-adjusted assessment.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Not established. A selected 2024 analysis found large increases in whole-lot assessments, but the frozen claim requires a 2016-2025 city-wide comparison for every replacement dwelling unit, including building-average values for units held on one title. That distribution has not been published and cannot be completed reliably from the open tables alone.
suggested_tldr: Whole-lot value often rises, but whole-lot value is not the verdict measure.
The public datasets lack reliable older completion dates and dwelling counts per title.
No source reports the required unit-level majority share or bounds.

claims.proposition_evaluated: Among separately titled replacement dwellings in the same matched 2016-2025 Edmonton teardown set, more than 50 percent would require shelter costs equal to or greater than 30 percent of monthly before-tax income for a hypothetical household earning the 2021 Census City of Edmonton median household income of $90,000 in 2020, using each dwelling's first arm's-length post-completion sale or first-full-roll total assessment and the brief's 20 percent down payment, price-month mortgage rate, 25-year amortization, property tax, utility and condominium-fee rules.
claims.interpretation_notes: This is a hypothetical purchase model, not evidence about actual occupants, purchaser incomes or rent affordability. Aggregate new-home and benchmark-price evidence is directionally informative but cannot replace the matched separately titled dwelling denominator. Single-title multi-unit dwellings were treated as excluded, not as affordable or unaffordable.

supporting_evidence.finding: The 2021 Census reports a median total household income of $90,000 in 2020 for the City of Edmonton and $96,000 for the Edmonton census metropolitan area.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Profile table, 2021 Census of Population: Edmonton City and Edmonton CMA
supporting_evidence.establishes: The primary and CMA income inputs specified by the brief.

supporting_evidence.finding: For 411 absorbed homeowner and condominium units in the City of Edmonton in 2025, CMHC reports a first-quintile price of $514,000, median of $592,500, fourth-quintile price of $725,000 and average of $617,939.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Average, Median and Price Percentiles for Absorbed Homeowner and Condominium Units by Census Subdivision
supporting_evidence.establishes: Most absorbed new homeowner and condominium units in Edmonton in 2025 sold well above the declared $90,000 household income. It is a strong directional comparator, but it does not isolate teardown replacements, separately titled dwellings or the full cohort.

supporting_evidence.finding: The City's 2024 market-housing report placed the Edmonton single- and semi-detached benchmark price at $431,100 and concluded it was likely out of reach for households earning less than $105,000.
supporting_evidence.establishes: A City analysis using different financing assumptions found that the declared $90,000 income was below its estimated income needed for the benchmark detached and semi-detached product. It does not establish the matched-cohort majority.

supporting_evidence.finding: Statistics Canada's standard classifies households spending 30 percent or more of total income on shelter costs in the claimed direction.
supporting_evidence.source_title: Classification of shelter cost to income ratio
supporting_evidence.establishes: The 30-percent classification in force on the freeze date.
supporting_evidence.quote: This category includes households who spend 30% or more of household total income on shelter costs.

challenging_evidence.finding: The same City report lists 2024 benchmark prices of $246,600 for townhouses and row houses and $181,200 for apartments, and says households earning more than $60,000 should be able to afford those benchmark types under its mortgage-qualification method.
challenging_evidence.establishes: Lower-priced housing types could fall below an affordability threshold for a $90,000 household. The share of those types in the separately titled teardown-replacement cohort therefore matters.

challenging_evidence.finding: The Bank of Canada discontinued its monthly chartered-bank interest-rate publication effective October 1, 2019. It states that historical monthly five-year conventional mortgage data remain under series V122521 and that weekly posted rates continue separately.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Changes to publication of interest rate statistics
challenging_evidence.establishes: The brief's price-month mortgage-rate input is not directly published as a monthly Bank of Canada series after September 2019. A predeclared rule for deriving a monthly value from weekly data is needed for later purchases.

challenging_evidence.finding: Statistics Canada Table 11-10-0222-01 publishes provincial household spending and a water, fuel and electricity category, with 2023 as the latest reference year released before the freeze date.
challenging_evidence.source_title: Household spending, Canada, regions and provinces
challenging_evidence.establishes: A provincial average utility allowance can be calculated, but it is not a cost observed for any replacement dwelling and could move cases near the threshold.

limitations: No public source identifies the complete set of separately titled replacement dwellings linked to eligible demolitions.
No open dataset supplies each dwelling's first arm's-length post-completion sale price and arm's-length status.
The City assessment data do not identify title form or publish the dwelling counts needed to separate the Claim 2 denominator from excluded single-title units.
No source reports the required city-wide or historical-Mature-Neighbourhood-Overlay numerator, denominator, bounds, bedroom breakdown or lot sensitivities.
The CMHC absorbed-price distribution covers all qualifying new homeowner and condominium units, not teardown-linked replacements.
The City's affordability report uses benchmark prices, income bands and a mortgage-qualification method rather than the frozen shelter-cost model.
Tenure, actual purchaser income, actual utilities and actual occupant shelter costs are unavailable. The model cannot describe what any occupant paid.
Property-level condominium fees are not available for a complete cohort.
CMHC survey rents may include or exclude utilities and cannot test rent affordability for the excluded single-title units.
The post-September-2019 monthly mortgage-rate input requires an aggregation choice not fixed in the brief.
unknowns: The number and share of replacement units that are separately titled.
The first qualifying sale price or first-full-roll assessed value for each separately titled replacement.
The number of condominiums and the condominium fee for each.
The complete price-year distribution and applicable mortgage and tax rates.
How many separately titled dwellings are unclassified and whether the resulting lower bound exceeds 50 percent.
Whether the conclusion differs in the mature-neighbourhood subset, five-year cohort, 30-year-amortization sensitivity or no-utility sensitivity.
The affordability of renting units excluded because they are held in single-title buildings.

missing_evidence.description: First arm's-length sale prices and dates for every separately titled replacement dwelling, linked to completion and title history.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: Alberta Land Titles, the REALTORS Association of Edmonton, property owners and purchasers

missing_evidence.description: Title form and verified dwelling count for every replacement building.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: Alberta Land Titles and City of Edmonton Development Services

missing_evidence.description: Property-level condominium fees for all condominium replacements.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: Condominium corporations, property owners, developers and listing services

missing_evidence.description: Prior and replacement tenure, contract rents and recorded tenant displacement.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: Property owners, tenants, developers and City of Edmonton program records

missing_evidence.description: A predeclared method for deriving price-month five-year conventional mortgage rates after the Bank ended the monthly series.
missing_evidence.likely_holder: YEGFacts editors using the Bank of Canada weekly series

calculations_needed: Construct the complete separately titled dwelling denominator from the matched Claim 1 frame and count excluded single-title dwelling units.
Select the first arm's-length sale after completion or first-full-roll total assessment for each tested dwelling.
For each price date, apply the declared five-year mortgage rate, 20 percent down payment and 25-year Canadian mortgage calculation.
Apply the City residential tax rate for the price year to the applicable assessed value.
Calculate the Alberta utility allowance from the latest Table 11-10-0222-01 categories and add published condominium fees.
Compare total monthly shelter cost with $2,250, which is 30 percent of the declared $90,000 annual income divided by 12.
Calculate the complete-denominator lower and upper bounds, unit and lot shares, bedroom breakdowns, and city-wide and mature-area results.
Repeat using the CMA income, regulatory-minimum down payment, 30-year amortization and no-utility sensitivities.
what_would_change_my_verdict: A reproducible complete-frame model showing that the lower bound exceeds 50 percent would change the verdict to Supported.
A reproducible model showing that the upper bound is 50 percent or less would change the verdict to Contradicted.
A linked transaction and title dataset, complete condominium-fee data and a fixed post-2019 mortgage-rate rule would permit the required calculation.
claims.suggested_one_line: New-home price evidence points toward a purchase-affordability problem for a $90,000 household, but the required matched, separately titled infill calculation and majority bounds are not available.
claims.suggested_short_answer: Not established. Edmonton's 2025 new-unit prices and the City's benchmark analysis support the claimed direction, but neither identifies the separately titled dwellings built on matched teardown lots. Missing title, sale, fee and mortgage-rate inputs prevent the required majority test.
suggested_tldr: The declared City median income is $90,000, making the modelled 30-percent limit $2,250 per month.
Recent new-home prices are directionally consistent with many dwellings failing that test.
The exact teardown-linked denominator and shelter-cost calculations have not been published.
